question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
Ruby gave her mother a hug and offered to knead the ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. flour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "knead" means to work flour and water (or other ingredients) into dough with the hands, so the word required in the blank must be "flour" — the powder made by grinding grain, used to make dough, bread, etc.

• "Flour" and "flower" are homophones — words that sound alike but have different spellings and meanings. Here, since Ruby is helping her mother in the kitchen (kneading), the sense clearly points to the baking ingredient "flour", not the blossom "flower".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "flora" means the plant life of a particular region or period; it does not fit the sense of kneading.

• Option 2: "flavour" means the distinctive taste of a food or drink; one cannot knead a "flavour".

• Option 3: "floor" refers to the lower surface of a room; it is unrelated to kneading and is also not a homophone of any word that fits here.

NOTE

• Common homophone pairs frequently asked in SSC exams: flour/flower, bare/bear, made/maid, mail/male, sail/sale, sea/see, sun/son, waist/waste, and hear/here.

• Always decide the correct homophone from the CONTEXT of the sentence, not merely from the sound of the word.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The line, 'Round the rugged rocks the ragged rascal ran' uses the repetition of usually initial consonant sounds in two or more neighbouring words or syllables .
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. alliteration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Alliteration" is a literary device defined as the repetition of usually initial consonant sounds in two or more neighbouring words or syllables. (एक ही व्यंजन ध्वनि की बार-बार पुनरावृत्ति)
◦ Example: In the line "Round the rugged rocks the ragged rascal ran", the consonant sound "r" is repeated at the start of several neighbouring words — this is alliteration.

• The underlined phrase in the question is, word for word, the standard dictionary definition of alliteration, so it must be substituted with this single term.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Epithet" (उपाधि/विशेषण): an adjective or descriptive phrase expressing a quality characteristic of the person or thing mentioned, e.g. "Alexander the Great". It has nothing to do with sound repetition.

• Option 3: "Simile" (उपमा): a figure of speech that directly compares two different things using "like" or "as", e.g. "as brave as a lion".

• Option 4: "Allegory" (रूपक कथा): a story, poem, or picture that can be interpreted to reveal a hidden moral or political meaning, e.g. Animal Farm.

NOTE

• Do not confuse alliteration with assonance (repetition of vowel sounds) or consonance (repetition of consonant sounds anywhere in neighbouring words, not just at the start).

• Other commonly tested literary devices: metaphor (implied comparison without "like/as"), onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds), personification (giving human qualities to non-human things), and hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The mother couldn’t ________ such an insult from her son in front of the others.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. bear.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "bear" means to tolerate, endure, or put up with something unpleasant. The sentence needs a word meaning "to tolerate an insult", so "bear" fits perfectly: "The mother couldn't bear such an insult from her son."

• "Bear", "bare", "beer" and "bier" are commonly confused because three of them (bare, beer, bier) sound close to "bear" but have entirely different meanings and spellings, so the correct word must be chosen strictly by MEANING, not sound.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "bier" is a movable frame on which a coffin or corpse is placed before burial; irrelevant here.

• Option 2: "bare" means uncovered or empty (e.g. bare feet, bare walls); it does not mean "to tolerate".

• Option 3: "beer" is an alcoholic drink made from fermented malt; it makes no sense in this sentence.

NOTE

• Remember the distinction: "bear" (verb) = to tolerate/carry, or (noun) = the animal; "bare" (adjective) = uncovered/empty.

• Other frequently confused word groups in SSC exams: their/there/they're, its/it's, whose/who's, and stationary/stationery.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
While I was walking to the store, my friend calls me and ask for a favour.
option_2: my friend calls me and ask
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. my friend calls me and ask.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "my friend" is a singular, third-person noun, so any verb agreeing with it in the Simple Present Tense must take the -s/-es ending. The sentence uses two verbs joined by "and" — "calls" and "ask" — both of which must agree with "my friend".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A singular subject in the third person takes a singular verb form (V1 + s/es) in the Simple Present Tense. Since "calls" is correctly used as "call + s", the second verb "ask" must also become "asks".

• Corrected segment: "my friend calls me and asks for a favour."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "While I was walking" is grammatically correct — the Past Continuous Tense is correctly used for a background action interrupted by another action.

• Option 3: "to the store" is a correct prepositional phrase; there is no error here.

• Option 4: "for a favour" is a correct prepositional phrase; there is no error here.

NOTE

• When two verbs are joined by "and"/"or" and share the same subject, BOTH verbs must independently agree with that subject in number and person.

• Common SSC trap: writers often correct the first verb but leave the second (or vice versa) in the wrong form — always check every verb governed by the same subject.

question:
Select the correct idiom to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
Due to her impoverished state, most of her relatives treated her with contempt.
option_2: Turned up their nose at her
option_4: Gave a wide space to her
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Turned up their nose at her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to turn up one's nose at someone/something" means to treat someone or something with contempt or disdain; to show scorn or disrespect. (किसी का तिरस्कार करना / नाक-भौं सिकोड़ना)
◦ Example: The rich relatives turned up their nose at the poor widow and her children.

• Since the sentence states that, because of her impoverished (poor) condition, her relatives "treated her with contempt", the idiom that exactly conveys this meaning is "turned up their nose at her".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Came in handy" (काम आना): to prove useful, especially in an unplanned way. Unrelated to contempt.

• Option 3: "Turned the corner at her" is not a standard idiom in this form — "turn the corner" actually means to pass the worst part of a difficult situation and start to improve; it has nothing to do with contempt.

• Option 4: "Gave a wide space to her" is not a recognised idiom; the correct expression is "to give someone a wide berth", meaning to avoid someone, which is different from showing contempt.

NOTE

• Other idioms of scorn/disrespect often tested: "to look down upon" (to consider inferior), "to give the cold shoulder" (to deliberately ignore someone), and "to snap one's fingers at" (to show defiant contempt).

• Do not confuse "turn up one's nose at" (show contempt) with "turn a blind eye to" (deliberately ignore a fault).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in the brackets to fill in the blank.
She left the party ______ because of her parents’ strict time restrictions. [late]
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. early.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word given in brackets is "late", which means happening or coming after the expected or usual time. Its antonym (opposite) is "early", meaning happening or coming before the expected time. (जल्दी / समय से पहले)
◦ Example: Because of her parents' strict time restrictions, she left the party early (rather than late).

• The sentence requires the OPPOSITE of "late" to logically complete the meaning: leaving "early" fits with parents' strict time restrictions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "exit" means to leave or go out; it is a verb/noun, not an antonym of "late", and is grammatically unsuitable after "left the party".

• Option 3: "small" means little in size; it is unrelated in meaning to "late".

• Option 4: "suffer" means to experience pain or hardship; it bears no opposite relationship to "late".

NOTE

• Common antonym pairs based on time, tested frequently in SSC: early/late, punctual/tardy, ahead/behind, and soon/eventually.

• Always confirm the antonym fits BOTH the meaning and the grammatical slot (part of speech) of the blank.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined group of words.
The soldier struck the enemy with the short sword fixed onto the end of the gun.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Bayonet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "bayonet" is a short sword or blade fixed onto (or near) the muzzle of a rifle/gun for use in close combat. (संगीन)
◦ Example: The soldiers fixed their bayonets before charging at the enemy trench.

• The underlined phrase "short sword fixed onto the end of the gun" is precisely the definition of a bayonet, so it is replaced by this one word.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Baron" (सामंत): a member of the lowest rank of nobility, or a powerful businessman (e.g. "oil baron"); unrelated to weapons.

• Option 3: "Bigot" (कट्टरपंथी): a person who is intolerant of opinions, races, or creeds different from their own.

• Option 4: "Baton" (डंडा): a stick carried by a police officer, or used in a relay race; it is not fixed onto a gun and is not a sword.

NOTE

• Other weapon-related one-word substitutions often asked: "Armistice" (a temporary agreement to stop fighting), "Ammunition" (a supply of bullets/shells), and "Arsenal" (a collection of weapons/place where they are stored).

• Be careful with words that sound similar but differ in meaning — Baron, Bigot, Baton and Bayonet are commonly confused as distractors in SSC OWS questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined word segment in the given sentence.
I picked up my little clock and it began to dance gracefully.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. chime prettily.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is a "little clock", and the verb phrase describing what a clock characteristically "does" — especially in a pleasing, musical way — is "to chime" (to ring its bell/mechanism to mark the time), not "dance" in the literal sense.

• The word "gracefully" in the original conveys a pleasant, attractive manner, which corresponds to "prettily" when applied to the pleasant sound a clock makes.

• Therefore, "began to dance gracefully", used figuratively for a clock, is best substituted by "began to chime prettily" — the clock started ringing its bell in a pleasant way.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "move gradually" does not capture the pleasant, musical sense implied by "gracefully"; "gradually" means slowly over time, which is not the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "lift smoothly" is unrelated — a clock chiming is not about being physically lifted.

• Option 4: "work agreeably" is too vague and generic; it does not specifically capture the pleasant ringing/chiming action associated with a clock.

NOTE

• Such questions test the ability to identify the CONTEXTUALLY appropriate substitute for a word/phrase used figuratively, rather than its dictionary-literal meaning.

• Clock-related vocabulary often tested: chime (ring melodiously), tick (make a light repeated sound), toll (ring slowly and solemnly, as a bell).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
We should clean the house regularly.
option_1: The house should have been cleaned regularly by us.
option_2: The house should be being cleaned regularly by us.
option_3: The house should be cleaned regularly by us.
option_4: The house should be clean regularly by us.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The house should be cleaned regularly by us.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "We should clean the house regularly" uses the modal auxiliary "should" with the base verb "clean".

• Rule — Passive Voice with Modals: Active: Subject + Modal + V1 + Object. Passive: Object + Modal + be + V3 + by + Subject.

• Applying the rule: the object "the house" becomes the subject; the modal "should" is retained; "be" is inserted before the past participle "cleaned"; and "we" becomes the agent "by us".
◦ Passive: The house should be cleaned regularly by us.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "should have been cleaned" is the passive form used for "should have + V3" (expressing an unfulfilled past obligation), which is not the tense of the original sentence.

• Option 2: "should be being cleaned" incorrectly uses a continuous passive form ("be being + V3"), which is not required here and is grammatically unnatural with "should".

• Option 4: "should be clean" wrongly uses the adjective "clean" instead of the past participle "cleaned"; passive voice always requires the V3 form of the main verb.

NOTE

• The structure "Modal + be + V3" is used for ALL modals (can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would) when converting an active sentence with a modal into the passive.

• Do not add "by us/by them" when the agent is not important or is obvious/generic — but retain it when explicitly present in the active sentence, as here.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct sequence to form a meaningful sentence.
(P) hard work and perseverance
(Q) no matter how difficult
(O) lead to success
(R) the journey may seem
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. POQR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part P ("hard work and perseverance") is the natural subject of the sentence, so it must come first.

• Part O ("lead to success") logically follows as the verb phrase completing the subject "hard work and perseverance", forming the core clause: "Hard work and perseverance lead to success."

• Parts Q ("no matter how difficult") and R ("the journey may seem") together form a concessive clause ("no matter how difficult the journey may seem") that must follow the main clause, modifying/qualifying it, with Q preceding R since "no matter how difficult" needs the following clause "the journey may seem" to complete its sense.

• Combining in the order P-O-Q-R gives a complete, meaningful sentence: "Hard work and perseverance lead to success no matter how difficult the journey may seem."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (ORQP) breaks the subject-verb link at the start ("lead to success... hard work"), producing an incoherent, backwards sentence.

• Option 3 (RPQO) starts with "the journey may seem", which cannot stand as the opening of the sentence without its introductory "no matter how difficult".

• Option 4 (RPOQ) similarly starts with part R, and disconnects the concessive clause (Q and R), which must stay together and in the order Q-R.

NOTE

• In parts-rearrangement questions, first identify the part that can stand as a natural SUBJECT and start the sentence with it, then look for a main clause before attaching subordinate/concessive clauses.

• Concessive markers like "no matter how", "although", "even though" always introduce a clause that needs a matching subject + verb immediately after (here, "the journey may seem").

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Summative assessment is the assignment of the student’s performance at the end of the academic term.
B. This new pattern ensures that besides just textbook teaching and learning, effective child-teacher interaction is encouraged.
C. The CBSE envisages two types of examinations, Formative and Summative.
D. Formative assessment is a part of the teaching-learning process and is done through conversation, quizzes, interviews, projects, assignments, etc.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. C, D, A, B.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C ("The CBSE envisages two types of examinations, Formative and Summative.") is the best opening sentence as it introduces the general topic — the two types of assessment — that the rest of the paragraph will explain.

• Sentence D ("Formative assessment is a part of the teaching-learning process...") logically follows C by explaining the FIRST type mentioned (Formative) in detail.

• Sentence A ("Summative assessment is the assignment of the student's performance at the end of the academic term.") follows D by explaining the SECOND type mentioned (Summative), maintaining the same order in which C introduced them.

• Sentence B ("This new pattern ensures that besides just textbook teaching and learning, effective child-teacher interaction is encouraged.") comes last as a concluding remark, using "This new pattern" to refer back to the Formative-and-Summative system just described in C, D and A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (B, C, A, D) wrongly opens with B, whose phrase "this new pattern" has no antecedent yet, making the opening incoherent.

• Option 2 (D, A, C, B) explains Formative and Summative (D, A) before C even introduces that there are two types of assessment, reversing the logical general-to-specific order.

• Option 3 (A, B, C, D) starts with the second-mentioned type (Summative) without any prior introduction, and misplaces B before the two types have even been explained.

NOTE

• In paragraph/sentence-rearrangement questions, look for a sentence that makes a GENERAL introductory statement (naming or introducing items) to serve as the opening, and check that any word like "this", "such", "these" has a clear antecedent in an earlier sentence.

• The order of explanation in the following sentences should mirror the order in which items were first introduced (here: Formative before Summative, matching C's "Formative and Summative").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word in bold.
The choice was judicious as further events proved.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. prudent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "judicious" means having, showing, or done with good judgement or sense; wise and sensible, especially in practical matters. (विवेकपूर्ण / समझदार)
◦ Example: The choice was judicious as further events proved — that is, the choice was wise/sensible, as later events confirmed.

• "Prudent" means acting with or showing care and thought for the future; sensible and wise — this matches the meaning of "judicious" most closely among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "silly" (मूर्खतापूर्ण): lacking good sense; foolish — this is the opposite of "judicious".

• Option 3: "hasty" (जल्दबाज़ी में किया गया): done with excessive speed or urgent haste, often without proper thought — the opposite of a judicious (well-considered) decision.

• Option 4: "ridiculous" (हास्यास्पद): deserving or inviting ridicule; absurd — again opposite in sense to "judicious".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "judicious": sensible, sound, shrewd, sagacious, discerning.

• Do not confuse "judicious" (wise) with "judicial" (relating to courts of law or judgement in a legal sense) — a very common SSC distractor pair.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The betrayer of the country was at last unmasked.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. traitor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "traitor" is a person who betrays their country, a friend, or a principle, especially by giving support to an enemy. (देशद्रोही)
◦ Example: The traitor who betrayed the country was at last unmasked.

• The underlined phrase "betrayer of the country" is exactly the meaning of "traitor", so it is replaced by this single word.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "truant" (स्कूल से नदारद रहने वाला): a student who stays away from school without permission; unrelated to betrayal.

• Option 3: "transgressor" (उल्लंघनकर्ता): a person who violates a law, command, or moral code; broader than betraying one's country specifically.

• Option 4: "theist" (आस्तिक): a person who believes in the existence of a god or gods; completely unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often tested: "Patriot" (one who loves and loyally supports their country — antonym of traitor), "Turncoat" (a person who changes their principles/loyalties, especially for personal advantage), and "Renegade" (a person who deserts a group or cause for a rival one).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Let the dust settle
option_1: To make use of a situation
option_2: Wait for the other person to make a move
option_4: To wait for a situation to become clear or certain
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To wait for a situation to become clear or certain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "let the dust settle" means to wait until a confusing, chaotic, or turbulent situation calms down and becomes clear before taking action. (स्थिति स्पष्ट होने तक इंतज़ार करना)
◦ Example: Let's let the dust settle after the merger before we decide on new roles.

• The idiom draws on the literal image of dust that has been kicked up (in an accident, argument, or upheaval) needing time to settle down before one can see clearly — figuratively, before the true state of affairs becomes clear.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To make use of a situation" describes an idiom like "to make hay while the sun shines" or "to seize the opportunity", not "let the dust settle".

• Option 2: "Wait for the other person to make a move" describes an idiom like "the ball is in their court", not "let the dust settle".

• Option 3: "To make a space tidy" takes the word "dust" too literally (as in housework), missing the idiomatic, figurative sense entirely.

NOTE

• Other idioms about waiting/patience often tested by SSC: "bide one's time" (wait patiently for the right opportunity), "sit tight" (wait patiently without acting), and "the ball is in your court" (it is now your turn to act/decide).

question:
Select the option that substitutes the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
In any time of crisis, there is always one mument that stands out from all the others.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. moment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads "...there is always one mument that stands out from all the others", where "mument" is a misspelling of the correct word "moment" — a very brief period of time. (क्षण)

• Spelling key: M-O-M-E-N-T. Note the vowel sequence "o" then "e" — the incorrect forms in the options wrongly rearrange or substitute these vowels/consonants (mumunt, mumont, momont).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "mumunt" — incorrect; both vowels are wrongly written as "u".

• Option 2: "mumont" — incorrect; the first "o" has been wrongly changed to "u".

• Option 3: "momont" — incorrect; the second vowel "e" has been wrongly changed to "o".

NOTE

• The related adjective is "momentary" (lasting only a moment) and "momentous" (of great importance) — do not confuse the spelling of these derived forms either.

• SSC frequently tests near-miss spellings of common words by swapping a single vowel or consonant — always sound out the word syllable by syllable (mo-ment) to check each part.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym for the underlined word in the given sentence.
It was his decency that he employed him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Courtesy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "decency" means behaviour that conforms to accepted standards of morality, politeness, or good taste. (शालीनता / भद्रता)
◦ Example: It was his decency that he employed him — that is, it was his courteous, well-mannered nature that led him to employ the person.

• "Courtesy" means polite, respectful behaviour — this matches the sense of "decency" most closely among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Rudeness" (अशिष्टता): offensively impolite or ill-mannered behaviour — the opposite of "decency".

• Option 2: "Deception" (धोखा): the act of deceiving someone; deliberately causing someone to believe something false. Unrelated to decency.

• Option 4: "Perversion" (विकृति): the alteration of something from its original meaning or state, or unacceptable/deviant behaviour — the opposite sense of "decency".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "decency": propriety, respectability, modesty, decorum.

• Do not confuse "decency" with its near-opposite "indecency" (improper or offensive behaviour) — a common SSC distractor pattern.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Please go and meet the chairperson. / She will be / away for the / few next days.
option_4: Please go and meet the chairperson.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. few next days.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "few next days" has the words in the wrong order. In English, when an ordinal-type word like "next" and a quantifier like "few" both modify a plural noun, the correct order is "next" + "few" + noun, i.e. "next few days", not "few next days".

• Rule — Order of pre-modifiers: Determiners/ordinal words such as next, last, first typically precede general quantifiers like few, many, several when both modify the same noun.

• Corrected segment: "She will be away for the next few days."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "She will be" is grammatically correct — Simple Future Tense correctly used.

• Option 2: "away for the" is grammatically correct with no error.

• Option 4: "Please go and meet the chairperson." is a correct imperative sentence with no error.

NOTE

• Similar word-order errors commonly tested by SSC: "last two weeks" (not "two last weeks"), "first three chapters" (not "three first chapters"); "next few days/weeks/months" is a fixed, natural collocation in English.

• Always read each segment independently and check it both for internal grammar and for correct word order.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
His father’s arm was bandaged by the kind nurse.
option_1: The kind nurse has bandaged his father’s arm.
option_2: The kind nurse had bandaged his father’s arm.
option_3: The kind nurse bandages his father’s arm.
option_4: The kind nurse bandaged his father’s arm.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The kind nurse bandaged his father's arm.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given passive sentence "His father's arm was bandaged by the kind nurse" is in the Simple Past Tense (was + V3).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense: Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject. Active: Subject + V2 + Object.

• Applying the rule: the agent "the kind nurse" becomes the subject; "was bandaged" becomes the simple past verb "bandaged"; and "his father's arm" becomes the object.
◦ Active: The kind nurse bandaged his father's arm.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "has bandaged" is the active form of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past Tense of the original sentence.

• Option 2: "had bandaged" is the active form of the Past Perfect Tense, which is not the tense used in the original passive sentence.

• Option 3: "bandages" is the active form of the Simple Present Tense, which does not match the past tense ("was bandaged") of the given sentence.

NOTE

• When converting passive to active, always first identify the TENSE of the passive verb group (here "was + V3" = Simple Past) and use the exact matching active tense — do not shift tense during conversion.

• The agent introduced by "by" in the passive sentence always becomes the SUBJECT of the active sentence.

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the ANTONYM of the underlined word from the given options.
I heard his suggestion but I am quite unsure about the risks involved in it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Certain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "unsure" means not confident or certain about something; having doubts. (अनिश्चित / संदेहयुक्त)
◦ Example: I heard his suggestion but I am quite unsure about the risks involved in it.

• The antonym (opposite) of "unsure" is "certain", meaning confident and having no doubt. (निश्चित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Thoughtful" (विचारशील): showing careful thought or consideration for others; not an antonym of "unsure".

• Option 2: "Interested" (रुचि रखने वाला): showing curiosity or concern about something; unrelated to certainty/doubt.

• Option 4: "Doubtful" (संदेहपूर्ण): this is actually a SYNONYM of "unsure" (both mean uncertain/having doubts), not its opposite — a common trap in antonym questions.

NOTE

• Other synonym/antonym pairs based on certainty often tested: sure/unsure, confident/hesitant, convinced/skeptical, definite/vague.

• Always eliminate options that are actually SYNONYMS (like "Doubtful" here) before selecting the true antonym — SSC frequently places a synonym as a distractor in antonym questions.

question: Select the sentence that contains a spelling error.
option_1: Fermented apple juice is touted to have many health benefits though most are anecdotal and not supported by scientific facts.
option_2: Intriguing as it is, the house was never sold because it was thought to be haunted.
option_3: It is important for scientists to acknowledge their humanity and the implications of their inventions.
option_4: There are many believes about ancient artefacts that some of them are patently not true.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. "There are many believes about ancient artefacts that some of them are patently not true."

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In this sentence, the word "believes" is used as a NOUN (meaning "things believed"), but "believe" is only a VERB in English (e.g. "I believe you"). The correct noun form is "beliefs" (plural of "belief").

• Corrected sentence: "There are many beliefs about ancient artefacts that some of them are patently not true."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Fermented apple juice is touted to have many health benefits though most are anecdotal and not supported by scientific facts." — no spelling error; all words correctly spelt.

• Option 2: "Intriguing as it is, the house was never sold because it was thought to be haunted." — no spelling error.

• Option 3: "It is important for scientists to acknowledge their humanity and the implications of their inventions." — no spelling error.

NOTE

• "Belief" (noun) and "believe" (verb) are a commonly confused noun-verb pair in English, similar to "advice" (noun) / "advise" (verb), and "practice" (noun) / "practise" (verb, in British English).

• In "spot the sentence with a spelling error" questions, the error is sometimes not a MISSPELLED word at all but a wrong WORD FORM (wrong part of speech) used in place of the correct one, as seen here.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The rise in global temperature (1)___________ already occurred is leading to extreme weather events that bring (2)___________ heat waves and droughts, devastating floods and increasingly powerful hurricanes and tropical storms. The combination of these factors means the impact on human health is increasing and is (3)___________ accelerate. But there is room for hope, particularly if governments take action now to (4)___________ the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021 and to go further in resolving the climate crisis. WHO is (5)___________ governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels and transition to a clean energy future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. that has.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the singular subject "the rise in global temperature", so the relative clause verb must agree in number with "rise" (singular) — the correct auxiliary is "has", not "have".

• Rule — Relative Pronoun + Present Perfect: A defining/restrictive relative clause describing a specific noun normally uses "that" (rather than "which", which more typically introduces non-defining clauses); and since the clause describes something "already occurred" up to now, the Present Perfect Tense (has + V3) is required: "that has already occurred".

• Complete phrase: "The rise in global temperature that has already occurred is leading to extreme weather events..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "which had" uses the Past Perfect ("had"), which wrongly implies the rise was completed before another past event, and "which" is less appropriate than "that" for this defining clause.

• Option 2: "that is" uses the Simple Present, which does not correctly convey that the rise has ALREADY occurred (a completed action with present relevance).

• Option 3: "which have" wrongly uses the plural auxiliary "have" with the singular subject "the rise", causing a subject-verb agreement error, apart from the same "which" vs "that" issue.

NOTE

• In restrictive/defining relative clauses referring to a singular noun, always match the auxiliary verb's number to the noun, not to any nearby plural word.

• "That" is generally preferred over "which" for defining relative clauses in formal/exam English, while "which" is reserved for non-defining (comma-separated) clauses.

The rise in global temperature (1)___________ already occurred is leading to extreme weather events that bring (2)___________ heat waves and droughts, devastating floods and increasingly powerful hurricanes and tropical storms. The combination of these factors means the impact on human health is increasing and is (3)___________ accelerate. But there is room for hope, particularly if governments take action now to (4)___________ the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021 and to go further in resolving the climate crisis. WHO is (5)___________ governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels and transition to a clean energy future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. intense.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes extreme weather events — "devastating floods" and "increasingly powerful hurricanes and tropical storms" — so the heat waves and droughts mentioned alongside them must also be described with a similarly strong, negative adjective. "Intense" (very strong or severe) fits this context of extreme weather.

• Rule — Contextual Word Choice: In cloze passages, the correct option must match not just the grammar of the sentence but also the overall TONE and MEANING established by the surrounding text (here, a passage about worsening/extreme climate events).

• Complete phrase: "...extreme weather events that bring intense heat waves and droughts, devastating floods and increasingly powerful hurricanes..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "mild" means not severe or strong — this contradicts the passage's tone of describing worsening, extreme weather.

• Option 3: "maximise" is a verb (meaning to make as great as possible) and cannot grammatically function as an adjective before the noun "heat waves".

• Option 4: "minor" means small or insignificant — this also contradicts the passage's description of extreme, devastating weather events.

NOTE

• In cloze passages about climate change, expect a consistently negative/severe tone throughout (words like intense, devastating, powerful, extreme) — use this tonal consistency to eliminate mismatched options like "mild" and "minor".

• Always check the part of speech required by the blank's position (here, an adjective before a noun) to quickly eliminate options like "maximise" (a verb).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The rise in global temperature (1)___________ already occurred is leading to extreme weather events that bring (2)___________ heat waves and droughts, devastating floods and increasingly powerful hurricanes and tropical storms. The combination of these factors means the impact on human health is increasing and is (3)___________ accelerate. But there is room for hope, particularly if governments take action now to (4)___________ the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021 and to go further in resolving the climate crisis. WHO is (5)___________ governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels and transition to a clean energy future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. likely to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...the impact on human health is increasing and is ___ accelerate." The structure "is likely to + base verb" is the standard way of expressing probability — that something is expected or probable to happen.

• Rule: "Likely to" + verb expresses probability/expectation, and it is the only one of the four options that makes logical and grammatical sense here, since the sentence is expressing a REASONABLE EXPECTATION that the impact will accelerate, not a negation of that likelihood.

• Complete phrase: "...the impact on human health is increasing and is likely to accelerate."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rarely to" is not a standard grammatical collocation ("is rarely to accelerate" is not idiomatic English) and contradicts the passage's warning tone.

• Option 3: "barely to" is likewise not a standard collocation with "is ___ accelerate", and "barely" (hardly at all) contradicts the passage's alarming tone about worsening health impacts.

• Option 4: "hardly to" is also not idiomatic in this structure, and "hardly" (almost not at all) again contradicts the sense that the impact is expected to worsen.

NOTE

• "Likely to" is a very common SSC cloze-test collocation expressing probability; contrast it with "unlikely to" (improbable), which would express the opposite sense.

• Adverbs like "rarely", "barely", and "hardly" are near-synonyms of near-negation and are frequently placed as distractors in passages with an urgent or alarming tone, where they do not fit logically.

The rise in global temperature (1)___________ already occurred is leading to extreme weather events that bring (2)___________ heat waves and droughts, devastating floods and increasingly powerful hurricanes and tropical storms. The combination of these factors means the impact on human health is increasing and is (3)___________ accelerate. But there is room for hope, particularly if governments take action now to (4)___________ the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021 and to go further in resolving the climate crisis. WHO is (5)___________ governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels and transition to a clean energy future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. honour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...governments take action now to ___ the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021..." The verb "honour" means to fulfil or keep to an agreement, obligation, or promise, which is exactly the collocation used with "pledges" — "to honour a pledge/promise".

• Rule — Collocation: Certain verbs pair naturally with certain nouns in formal English; "honour" is the standard, formal collocate of "pledge", "commitment", "agreement", and "promise".

• Complete phrase: "...governments take action now to honour the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "take" does not collocate naturally with "pledges" in the sense of fulfilling them — "to take a pledge" would mean to make a NEW promise, not to fulfil an existing one already made at Glasgow.

• Option 3: "watch" means to observe; it does not carry any sense of fulfilling an obligation.

• Option 4: "keep" can sometimes collocate with "promise" ("keep a promise"), but in this formal context about international climate commitments, "honour the pledges" is the more precise and standard usage intended by the passage.

NOTE

• Common formal collocations tested by SSC: "honour a commitment/agreement/pledge", "fulfil an obligation", "keep one's word", "break a promise".

• Pay attention to REGISTER (level of formality) in cloze passages — formal/journalistic passages (like this WHO-related text) favour formal collocations such as "honour" over more casual alternatives.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The rise in global temperature (1)___________ already occurred is leading to extreme weather events that bring (2)___________ heat waves and droughts, devastating floods and increasingly powerful hurricanes and tropical storms. The combination of these factors means the impact on human health is increasing and is (3)___________ accelerate. But there is room for hope, particularly if governments take action now to (4)___________ the pledges made at Glasgow in November 2021 and to go further in resolving the climate crisis. WHO is (5)___________ governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels and transition to a clean energy future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. calling on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "WHO is ___ governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels..." The phrasal verb "to call on someone to do something" means to formally appeal to or urge someone to take a particular action.

• Rule — Phrasal Verb Collocation: "Call on" + person/organisation + "to" + verb is the standard structure for making a formal appeal or urging action — exactly the sense needed here, where WHO is urging governments to act.

• Complete phrase: "WHO is calling on governments to lead a just, equitable, and fast phase out of fossil fuels..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "calling at" means to stop briefly at a place (e.g. "the train calls at every station"); it does not mean appealing to someone to act.

• Option 3: "calling for" means demanding or requiring something (e.g. "the situation calls for caution") and is not usually followed by a person + infinitive in this appealing sense; "calling on governments to lead" is the correct, more precise collocation for urging a specific party to act.

• Option 4: "calling from" would indicate the place a call originates from (e.g. "calling from London"); it makes no grammatical or logical sense here.

NOTE

• Common phrasal verbs with "call" tested by SSC: "call on" (appeal/urge/formally visit), "call off" (cancel), "call for" (demand/require), "call up" (telephone someone, or summon for military service), "call in" (ask for help/withdraw a request).

• "Call on someone to do something" is a very common structure in formal/journalistic English when reporting appeals made by organisations, officials, or governments.
